connector: Anne’s story is finished, and a new book is waiting: Number the Stars. It happens in Denmark in 1943, in the middle of a war. Before we open it, we spend four days on the real history underneath it. Today starts with the biggest question of all: how did the war begin, and who started it?

transcripts.welcome: Welcome. You’ve just said goodbye to Anne and Green Gables, and a new book is close. Before we open it, we spend this week on the true history behind it. Today’s question is how World War Two began, and who started it. First you’ll warm up and do some word work. Then a short reading, and a few questions to answer in your own words.
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is a bit like packing for a trip. A novel set in real history expects you to bring some facts along. As you read, collect the names of countries, leaders, and dates, like things going into a suitcase. When the story starts next week, you’ll be glad they’re already packed.
transcripts.dol: The top sentence is a model, and every capital in it is there for a reason. Look at the names of places, months, and people. The bottom one has lost all of its capitals, and it’s really two sentences squeezed into one. Find where one thought ends and the next one begins.
transcripts.guide1: Four kinds of word work today. Some of it asks you to notice before anyone tells you the rule, and that’s on purpose. A rule you find yourself stays with you longer than one you’re handed. So go slowly at the start, look hard, and make your best guess before you check.
transcripts.morphology: This week we’re building a bridge, one word at a time. Two small word parts at the front of words will do the building. One means across, and one means forward. Read each meaning first, then choose the part that fits. Every right choice lays a plank. By the end of the week, the bridge will reach the other shore.
transcripts.vocabulary: These four words will follow you all through the new book. Each one is about what can happen to a country, and to the people in it, during a war. Read the sentence, take the word apart, then make your guess before you flip the card. Guessing first is how a word starts to belong to you.
transcripts.grammar: Some words stand in for people: she, they, him, them. They don’t all do the same job. Some do the action, some receive it, and a couple can do both. Sort them by the job they’re doing, then name the groups yourself. Names you give stick better than names you’re given.
transcripts.spelling: Long words from history often hide two vowels working together to make one sound. The trick is that the same pair doesn’t always sound the same. Say each word out loud, slowly, and listen for what the pair is really saying before you sort it. Your ear knows more than you think.
transcripts.copia: Here is one plain sentence about the end of the war. Your job is to say it three different ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. Writers have practiced this way for hundreds of years. Each new way shows you something the first sentence left out.
transcripts.guide2: This quarter we watch for courage, and here is the first thing to know about it. Courage isn’t the same as not being scared. It’s being scared and doing the right thing anyway. Even reading about a hard time in history takes a little of that. If today’s facts feel heavy, that’s all right. Stay with them. That’s the first small brave thing.
transcripts.read: The passage is short, and it covers six long years. Watch for two things: the countries that were taken over, one after another, and the countries that joined together to stop it. When you reach the pause questions, stop and think about a child your age living in one of those places.
transcripts.guide3: Now it’s your turn to write. The questions ask you to go back to the passage, so keep it open beside you. Use the passage’s own facts, the dates and the names, to show how you know. Then you’ll finish with a short piece of your own writing.
transcripts.chapter: These three questions build on each other. The first asks when and who. The second asks what was happening. The third asks who stood against it. Put them together, and you have the whole shape of the war in a few sentences. That shape is what you’ll carry into the novel.
transcripts.workshop: Your writing project this quarter is an opinion essay, and it starts with one simple skill. A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks, and someone else could disagree. Today you’ll practice telling them apart, using things from your own life. Soon you’ll use the same skill on the new book.

a.raw: the war began in europe in 1939 hitler led the german army
a.fixed: The war began in Europe in 1939. Hitler led the German army.
a.why: Capital T to start, a capital on Europe, a period after the year, a capital H on Hitler, a capital G on German, and a period at the end.

b.raw: the allies fought against germany britain and france were two of them
b.fixed: The Allies fought against Germany. Britain and France were two of them.
b.why: Capitals on The, Allies, Germany, Britain and France, a period after Germany, and a period at the end. Allies takes a capital here because it names one group.

scholar.journal-q1: … and tell how many years the war lasted from start to finish.
scholar.journal-q2: … and say what those invasions tell you about Hitler’s goal.
scholar.journal-q3: … and explain why it mattered that so many countries joined together.

match.occupation: Occupation is about one country taking control of another. Look for the meaning about taking over.
match.resistance: Resistance means pushing back. Look for the meaning about standing up against something wrong.
match.deport: Deport is about being sent out of a country. Look for the meaning about being forced to leave.
match.rescue: To rescue someone is to get them out of danger. Look for the meaning about saving.

sort.she: She is the one doing something: she ran, she spoke. Try it at the start of a sentence.
sort.her: Her is who something happens to: the soldier saw her. Try it after the action word.
sort.they: They does the action: they marched. Try it at the start of a sentence.
sort.them: Them receives the action: the soldiers stopped them. Try it after the action word.
sort.you: You never changes: you saw it, and it saw you. Which column fits a word that does both jobs?
sort.it: It never changes either: it fell, and we found it. Which column fits a word that does both jobs?
sort.achieve: Say it slowly: a-CHEEVE. What sound does the middle make?
sort.campaign: The end of campaign rhymes with rain. Which sound is that?
sort.neutral: Neutral starts like new. That isn’t a long E or a long A.
sort.retreat: Retreat ends like treat. What sound is in the middle of treat?
sort.betrayal: Betrayal has a word inside it that rhymes with day. Which sound is that?
sort.mountain: Say mountain the way you normally would. The second part goes soft and quick. Is that a clear long A?

copia.seed: The war finally ended in 1945, when the Allies defeated Germany.
eg: After six long years, the war finally ended in 1945, when the Allies defeated Germany.
The war finally stopped in 1945, when the Allies defeated Germany.
The war finally ended in 1945, when the Allies defeated Germany in Europe.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Each right word lays a plank and the bridge reaches forward.

why.t: This week is a bridge between two books, from Anne’s island to Denmark, where Number the Stars takes place. trans- means across, so each word lays a plank across the water. pro- means forward, so the bridge reaches forward, one span each lesson, until it touches the far shore.

wordgame.win: The bridge reaches the far shore, and every lamp is lit. trans- = across, pro- = forward. Next week, the story begins.

notes.wgrd: Before reading historical fiction, build background knowledge: collect the names, places and dates the story will expect you to know, and ask what each one meant for a child living then.
vocab: Standing up against something you believe is wrong.
When one country takes over and controls another.
To force someone to leave a country, usually against their will.
notes.wordParts: trans- means “across” or “through” (transport, translate). pro- means “forward” (progress, protect).
notes.grammar: Subject pronouns do the action: I, he, she, we, they. Object pronouns receive it: me, him, her, us, them. You and it can do both. Test: swap in he or him.
notes.spelling: A vowel team is two letters making one sound: ie and ea can say a long E (achieve, retreat); ai and ay can say a long A (campaign, betrayal). In a quick, unstressed part of a word a team can go soft, like the ai in mountain.
